hits.snippet: Deeptech startup Discovered Materials has raised $9 million (approximately ₹85 crore) in a seed funding round led by Lightspeed India Partners, with participation from Y Combinator, Peak XV Partners and others. Founded by IIT Madras alumni Akash Ramdas and Advaith Sridhar, the San Francisco-based startup is building AI systems that can accelerate the materials discovery process from simulation and synthesis to laboratory validation. The fresh capital will be used to expand the team, build laboratory infrastructure and advance its AI agents, with an initial focus on materials for advanced semiconductor applications. Read full news here: [...] Discovered Materials has raised a $9 million seed round to find materials that let computer chips run cooler. TechCrunch reported on August 10 that Lightspeed India Partners led the round, with Peak XV Partners and angels including Paul Graham and Gokul Rajaram also investing. The startup came out of Y Combinator. The pitch: point AI agents at one narrow problem instead of materials discovery broadly. hits.title: Discovered Materials is playing AI whack-a-mole to hunt cooler chips
hits.snippet: Tim Fernholz Chips running AI workloads are too hot: That’s one reason why data centers consume so much electricity and require cooling systems. And, inevitably, entrepreneurs are turning to AI to solve the problem it created. Discovered Materials is the latest, with plans to use swarms of AI agents to find new materials that can be used to build more efficient integrated circuits. The startup said it recently closed a $9 million seed round from Lightspeed India Partners after emerging from from Y Combinator, with investment from Peak XV Partners and angel investors Paul Graham, Gokul Rajaram, and Thariq Shihipar. [...] One challenge is the engineering trade-space: If they find a material that might reduce heat generation or improve dissipation, it might be too difficult to actually manufacture a chip out of it, or its electrical properties are compromised. “It’s a bit of playing whack-a-mole with atomic structures,” Hemant Mohapatra, the Lightspeed partner who led this round, told TechCrunch. “A material is only useful in the real world if all of them converge at once, which is what makes this a really interesting search problem.”
